There are dozens of main branches of the influenza virus family. And it mutates at a crazy rate. It's difficult to guess what strains will give the largest infection rates from year to year in time to create the vaccine, but epidemiologists do their best given the data they have to work with. The vaccine changes yearly, being designed to confer immunity from whatever they expect to be the worst strains. This grants immunity from those particular strains, as well as partial immunity to closely related strains. Over the years, after repeated exposures in the form of vaccines, a person has partial immunity to many strains. The value of the flu vaccine lies in that broad spectrum protection, not necessarily in a promise that getting the vaccine this year will prevent you from getting any flu this year.

During the last major outbreak of avian influenza, my city saw their worst morbidity and mortality among people in their twenties and thirties. Middle aged adults had lived through the outbreak in the seventies and had partial immunity, and as a population tended to fare much better.

Childhood vaccinations require periodic boosters to keep immunity.
